data.title: The Fed is unlikely to rescue the AI trade
data.description:
Markets have been handed a breather. European shares rose sharply this morning, with the Stoxx 600 up 1.6% by 9:24 a.m. in London, and Asian chipmakers bounced after a bruising Wednesday.

US exchanges are shut for Thanksgiving, so nobody can yet test whether Wall Street's late recovery on Wednesday will hold.

It would be a mistake to read the rebound as the start of a rescue.

My argument is simple: the Federal Reserve is unlikely to come to the aid of the AI trade, because the AI build-out is not a bystander in the inflation fight. It is one of the causes.

Start with Wednesday's data. The PCE price index, the Fed's preferred gauge, rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, nearly twice the 2% target.

Core PCE came in at 3.3%, a tenth above forecasts, according to CNBC and the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).

Growth does not argue for caution either. The BEA revised third-quarter GDP up to 4.3% annualised from 3.4%, reflecting stronger business investment and consumer spending.

Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials treat as a key read on underlying demand, rose 5.8%. Jobless claims fell to 189,000.

Now the Fed's own words. The minutes of its October meeting, which held rates at 3.75% to 4%, show many participants viewed the AI build-out as a material source of inflation risk.

Demand for AI-related products, they noted, was straining supply and pushing up the prices of technology goods.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh made the same point at his October press conference, pushing back against the idea that AI investment is insulated from monetary policy.

"Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything," Warsh said.

He argued that higher borrowing costs were already influencing investment decisions across the technology sector, challenging the assumption that AI's expected returns make it immune to tighter financial conditions.

Yet the bond market is betting on a different story. Futures imply a 98% chance of a quarter-point hike on December 8-9, 2026, but the 10-year Treasury yield is near 4.85% after touching an 11-week low overnight.

The 10-year inflation breakeven is about 2.1%. After the PCE release, CNBC reported, the odds of a third hike in 2027 fell to roughly one in three from even.

Investors, in other words, are wagering that the sell-off will do the Fed's work for it.

The strongest counterargument deserves a fair hearing. Bloomberg reported that the Nasdaq 100 fell 20% from its early October record, erasing more than $8.5 trillion.

The financing behind the boom looks fragile: the Financial Times reported that the five big hyperscalers committed $33 billion more to capital spending than they generated from operations, the first time their combined free cash flow had turned negative.

Fed staff flagged off-balance-sheet and circular AI financing, and almost every participant worried about disappointing returns. If credit seizes, the Fed would have to respond.

That is right as far as it goes, but I see three problems with leaning on it.

First, scale. At its Wednesday low, Bloomberg reported, the Nasdaq 100 was down just 0.6% for the year, and the S&P 500 closed only 0.25% lower. That is a correction in a rich market, not yet a wealth shock.

Second, sequence. Central banks stop tightening when something breaks, not when prices fall. Fed staff judged the financial system resilient, with well-capitalised banks.

The minutes describe stress severe enough to impair market functioning only in "very severe scenarios".

Third, credibility. Inflation has run above target for around 5½ years, CNBC noted, and the committee's stated line is that it "will deliver price stability".

A Fed that holds that line cannot ease because chip stocks are down.

There is an irony here. The minutes say greater scrutiny of AI returns and financing could slow spending and so reduce inflation pressure.

Relief for the Fed arrives through lower AI capital spending, not despite it. The adjustment the market hopes will save it is the one that hurts it most.

For investors, the implication is uncomfortable. A high discount rate and a wobbling capital-spending cycle hit the same assets from two sides.

Wednesday's late buying shows appetite for bargains, not proof of a backstop.

Oil adds to the strain, with Brent at about $95 a barrel on Middle East supply fears, and tariff risk lingers. This is analysis, not a recommendation.

What to watch next? First, the December 8-9, 2026 Fed meeting, for the size of the move and any shift in the 2027 path. Then the next PCE release on December 23, 2026.

Beyond that, watch hyperscaler spending plans and debt issuance for 2027, and S&P's review of Nvidia's credit rating.

Finally, watch whether oil and tariffs push inflation higher still: OPEC+ meets on November 29, 2026, and the tariff comment period closes on January 5, 2027.

The test of this view is simple: if the Fed skips December while core inflation is still 3.3%, I am wrong.

data.title: Nasdaq, Dow rise over 500 pts as Anthropic pops 11% to lead AI rebound
data.description:
US stocks rallied on Friday as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday and bought beaten-down technology shares in a shortened session.

The Dow rose 592 points, or 1.18%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6%. The Nasdaq 100 jumped 2.61% as investors sought bargains in some of the market's worst-performing technology stocks.

The shortened Black Friday session provided some relief after a turbulent week in which concerns about AI spending, rising borrowing costs and regulatory risks triggered sharp swings across Wall Street.

Despite recent volatility, all three benchmarks posted strong weekly gains.

The Dow was up more than 5% in its biggest weekly rise since October 2022 and the S&P 500 also recorded its best week since April 2025.

The Nasdaq made its largest weekly gain since April with a surge of more than 6%.

Anthropic leads AI rebound

Anthropic shares jumped nearly 11% to $91.88, moving comfortably above their $83 IPO price after a volatile first week as a publicly traded company.

The Claude maker had briefly fallen below its IPO valuation amid concerns about its enormous infrastructure spending commitments and the financing required to sustain its expansion.

Other AI-related stocks also rallied.

Sandisk surged 16%, while Micron gained 7.6%. AMD advanced 4.6%, Broadcom added 3.8% and Meta climbed 3.1%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index also gained 4.69% as investors returned to chipmakers and data-center hardware companies.

"The market is so oversold that a bounce was inevitable," Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group, was quoted as saying by Reuters.

Nvidia scrutiny intensifies

Even as other chip stocks surged, Nvidia was among the notable exceptions for almost the entire session before it pared losses towards the end to finish 0.80% higher.

Despite the gains, the chipmaking giant remains under pressure.

A Bloomberg report revealed that Chinese companies had installed Nvidia's powerful Blackwell processors at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese agent at the centre of the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.

The facility reportedly contained a GB300 NVL72 rack and a GB200 server, raising fresh questions about how restricted American AI processors reached China.

The development adds to Nvidia's existing regulatory and political challenges. S&P Global Ratings has placed its AA credit rating on CreditWatch Negative over management and governance concerns.

Jensen Huang is also scheduled to face congressional questioning between December 1 and December 3 over export controls, corporate governance, and the company's dealings in Asia.

SpaceX and Tesla shares gain

SpaceX shares climbed nearly 5%, partly supported by Elon Musk's decision to expand his share giveaway programme for American children.

Musk said he would donate another SpaceX share to every child in the US each year, building on an earlier commitment by the company and Musk to provide shares worth an estimated $18 billion.

Tesla shares jumped nearly 5% in Friday's trading after Germany’s antitrust regulator disclosed a filing for the electric-vehicle maker to acquire assets from EMAG – a German supplier of precision manufacturing equipment.

The proposed transaction offers a clue to how the EV maker might tackle one of the toughest parts of commercializing Optimus, its humanoid robot.

Bloomberg previously reported that negotiations between Musk's two companies for a merger were progressing, potentially setting up one of the largest corporate transactions ever.

Fed rate bets and tariffs remain headwinds

Despite Friday's recovery, macroeconomic concerns remain.

Markets are pricing in approximately 99% odds of a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate increase at the December 8-9 meeting as inflation remains above target.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration's proposal for additional tariffs on imports from 14 trading partners has introduced another source of uncertainty.

Oil prices were down, with WTI dropping 0.86% to under $83 a barrel while Brent slipped towards $94 with a decline of 2.5%.

data.title: Why Tesla shares jumped 5% on Friday?
data.description:
Tesla (TSLA) shares jumped nearly 5% higher in Friday's trading after Germany’s antitrust regulator disclosed a filing for the electric-vehicle maker to acquire assets from EMAG – a German supplier of precision manufacturing equipment.

The proposed transaction offers a clue to how the EV maker might tackle one of the toughest parts of commercializing Optimus, its humanoid robot.

The same gearing that lets a prototype move smoothly has to work “reliably” across thousands of machines, at a cost customers can justify. EMAG makes equipment designed to help manufacturers do that.

Tesla stock is currently down some 9% year-to-date.

Why EMAG matters for Tesla stock

Germany’s Federal Cartel Office listed the Nov. 23 filing as an asset acquisition under review. The public entry leaves the price and the specific assets involved undisclosed.

EMAG’s specialty is equipment that cuts, shapes and finishes metal parts to exacting tolerances, including the gears and screws used in actuators, the mechanisms that move a robot’s joints.

Bringing some of that expertise in-house could let Tesla’s engineers adjust a part and test how well it can be manufactured without waiting for an outside supplier to retool.

For investors, that offers a practical way to shorten development cycles and gain more control over a critical part of the Optimus supply chain.

How EMAG strengthens long-term case for TSLA

Tesla said in its latest quarterly filing that it was preparing for large-scale Optimus production.

EMAG’s equipment could help with the economics of that ramp. A humanoid robot needs multiple actuators, so a modest saving on each can add up across an entire machine.

Tighter control over machining could also reduce the number of parts that need to be scrapped or reworked, improving factory output without a proportionate increase in spending.

Those gains could give Tesla more room to price Optimus competitively.

The financial payoff still depends on how quickly Tesla can integrate the assets and whether customers find enough work for the robots to justify buying them in volume.

An EU driving vote is the next date to watch

Friday’s rally in TSLA shares also came as a draft European Commission agenda pointed to a possible Dec. 15 vote on Tesla’s supervised driving system.

Approval could widen the market for the software across the European Union, giving Tesla a nearer-term commercial opportunity while Optimus ramps up.

The prospect of a Tesla-SpaceX merger also remained in the background. Both companies have disclosed special committees, and the Financial Times reported this week that advisers are modeling a possible all-stock deal.

For investors following EMAG specifically, the next detail worth watching is which assets Tesla would acquire. That will help establish how much manufacturing capability Tesla could bring in-house and how much it would still need to build.

data.title: Why Nvidia pared opening gains to decline again on Friday?
data.description:
Nvidia NVDA shares reversed their opening gains on Friday as fresh reports about the presence of its advanced Blackwell processors at a Chinese data center linked to Alice Huang added to mounting concerns around the chipmaker.

The stock had initially risen 3% at the opening bell as investors bought beaten-down technology shares following the Thanksgiving holiday. However, it soon went down and remained in the red at the time of writing, down 0.25% at 12:18 ET.

The dip made Nvidia one of the notable laggards during an otherwise positive shortened session for technology stocks.

All three major benchmarks were up more than 1%, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite leading the gains with a 1.81% rise.

However, Nvidia's tough times continued as the stock was in the red for the third straight session after Jensen Huang's return had pushed shares 31.5% higher in a stunning rally.

Fresh concerns emerge for Nvidia

A Bloomberg report on Friday revealed that two Chinese companies installed Nvidia's powerful Blackwell processors at a Shanghai data center connected to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy at the centre of the controversy surrounding the chipmaker's CEO.

The Yangtze River Delta Project facility included a GB300 NVL72 server rack, one of Nvidia's most powerful computing systems.

According to documents reviewed by Bloomberg, Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to secure a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank.

A second company, Shanghai Kezhan, also listed a GB200 server at the facility in documents relating to a separate 90 million yuan loan.

The connections to Alice Huang run through Singapore-based Megaspeed, the cloud computing company she founded in 2023 and which became one of Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customers.

Shanghai Shuoyao confirmed that it was one of Megaspeed's service providers, although it described the relationship as limited to ordinary commercial cooperation.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in response to the US investigation.

To be sure, Bloomberg said it had no evidence that Megaspeed diverted the Nvidia hardware to China.

However, the chips are subject to US export restrictions and cannot be shipped to Chinese companies without a licence. That makes it a subject of concern for Nvidia.

Southeast Asia chip halt could be expensive

The Bloomberg report follows another potentially damaging development involving Nvidia's business in Southeast Asia.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Nvidia had instructed manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, to halt shipments of servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

The restrictions follow tighter US export controls introduced last week to prevent Chinese companies from accessing advanced AI computing capacity through cloud service providers in the region.

Nvidia booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72% increase from a year earlier, according to the Financial Times.

Jefferies estimates that the new restrictions could put between $44 billion and $62 billion of Nvidia's data center revenue at risk next year.

UBS believes the rules could affect as much as 2GW of new data center demand, although the brokerage said the eventual impact remained difficult to quantify.

Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, estimates that the restrictions could reduce Nvidia's 2027 revenue by 2% to 5%.

Worries pile up for Nvidia

S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on CreditWatch Negative on Wednesday, citing concerns about management and governance, including board independence, oversight of executive conduct and succession planning.

The agency said Huang's departure and subsequent reinstatement had not adequately addressed its concerns. A downgrade could follow within 90 days.

Congressional scrutiny is also intensifying.

Huang is scheduled to appear before three House committees for transcribed interviews on December 1, while Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is due to appear the following day.

The CEO will also face a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.

data.title: Warren Pies says recent market sell-off not because of AI
data.description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have taken some of the hardest hits in the recent market sell-off, but Warren Pies of 3Fourteen Research says the Federal Reserve deserves most of the blame.

Speaking on CNBC on Nov. 25, Pies called the Fed’s hawkish stance “the proximate cause of most of this weakness.”

He sees interest-rate policy driving stocks over the next three to six months and would wait for evidence that the Fed is ready to ease up before calling a market bottom.

Even so, Pies said he’d buy beaten-down AI stocks with a long enough time horizon.

Higher inflation makes a 2018-style rescue harder

Warren Pies drew a parallel with late 2018, when stocks found a floor after traders stopped pricing in further rate hikes for 2019.

Then-Fed Chair Jerome Powell reinforced that shift in early January by signaling patience. Pies is looking for a similar sequence this time, with policymakers confirming what traders are starting to price in. Chorus

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has less room to make that turn, in Pies’ view.

The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year over year in October, and core inflation was 3.3%. Pies contrasted that with inflation of around 2% at the end of 2018, when the Fed had an easier case for pausing.

A relief rally could make a Fed pause harder

Pies said rates traders were moving toward pricing in a Dec. hike followed by a pause. He was skeptical the Fed would validate that outlook.

A sharp stock rally ahead of the meeting could itself complicate the decision. Rising share prices can loosen financial conditions, giving policymakers more room to keep tightening while inflation remains elevated.

“Rallies can be self-defeating,” Pies said. He pointed to rebounds during the 2018 and 2022 tightening cycles as reasons to be wary of calling a bottom on the strength of a bounce.

For him, a clearer signal would come from the Fed’s own guidance.

Why Pies would still buy beaten-down AI stocks

Pies is watching Anthropic’s $83 IPO price as a gauge of investor appetite for AI. He said a break below that level could make investors question whether OpenAI could go public in this market.

The concern extends beyond Anthropic shareholders. A weak debut can make it harder for other AI companies to raise money on favorable terms.

Still, Pies sees a growing range of uses for AI agents and doubts the sell-off marks the start of a dot-com-style bear market.

Pies wants more evidence that stocks have found a floor before buying on a short-term basis. His view changes when he looks further out. “When you zoom out a year from now, it’s a buy,” he said.

data.title: Switzerland’s first spot bitcoin ETF debuts on SIX with 350 BTC in assets
data.description:
Switzerland’s first exchange-traded fund to invest directly in bitcoin has begun trading on SIX Swiss Exchange, giving investors in the country a fund-based alternative to the debt-style crypto products that dominate Europe.

The Bitcoin Fund ETF, ticker BBIT, listed on November 26, 2026, SIX said in a media release. Pernet von Ballmoos AG (PvB) is the issuer and fund management company, while BIT Asset Management is sponsor, asset manager and distributor.

BIT Asset Management, the Zurich-based subsidiary of Singapore-headquartered digital asset platform BIT, formerly Matrixport, said the fund launched with 350 bitcoin in assets. The Block put the value of that holding at more than $20 million.

A fund rather than a note

The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) approved the fund on October 20, 2026, describing it as the first exchange-traded retail fund in Switzerland to invest directly in bitcoin.

FINMA classified it as an “other fund for alternative investments” with a specific risk under Swiss law. It granted an exemption from the usual risk diversification rules, citing bitcoin’s long trading history and high trading volume.

BIT Asset Management said the approval followed an 18-month review. FINMA added that other fund providers have also submitted or announced applications for bitcoin ETFs.

The distinction matters because most bitcoin products listed in Europe are exchange-traded products (ETPs). These are debt instruments that carry the credit risk of their issuer, BIT noted.

BBIT, by contrast, is a Swiss investment fund governed by the Collective Investment Schemes Act (CISA). Its assets are legally segregated, and investors hold fund units rather than a claim on the issuer.

The fund’s bitcoin is held in segregated cold storage at AMINA Bank, a FINMA-regulated Swiss bank, according to BIT. The fund does not use derivatives or securities lending.

“The economic exposure of a fund and a note can look very similar when everything goes well. The difference is what happens when it doesn’t,” said Friedrich Herzog, chief investment officer of BIT Asset Management.

In the EU, retail funds under UCITS rules generally cannot hold a single crypto asset directly, which has left ETPs as the main listed route to bitcoin for European investors. BIT describes BBIT as currently Europe’s only spot bitcoin ETF.

How investors can access it

BBIT trades in both Swiss francs and US dollars, with Flow Traders acting as market maker. It tracks the SIX Reference Rate Bitcoin Index, and the minimum investment is one unit.

The fund carries a total expense ratio of 0.19% a year, BIT said. Eligible investors can also subscribe in kind by contributing bitcoin directly, subject to the prospectus.

Its public offering is limited to Switzerland, and it is not available to US persons. BIT said it can be bought via banks, brokers and investment platforms with SIX access, without a digital wallet or crypto exchange account.

The Block reported that BIT pointed to investors outside the US, including Asian clients of Swiss private banks, as a potential audience. It did not specify which investors outside Switzerland could buy the fund.

“If investors want a US product, they have plenty of choice. If they want a non-US product in a neutral jurisdiction, until now they really didn’t,” said Cynthia Wu, co-founder and chief commercial officer of BIT.

Launch into a weak market

The listing comes during a difficult period for bitcoin. US spot bitcoin ETFs recorded about $4.94 billion of net outflows in November through November 24, according to SoSoValue data cited by The Block.

FINMA has warned that bitcoin investments remain highly risky even through an approved ETF. It said providers must give clear risk warnings and pay close attention to suitability under the Financial Services Act (FinSA).

For investors who prefer direct ownership, Invezz’s guide on how to buy bitcoin compares the main routes.

With the listing, the number of ETF issuers on SIX Swiss Exchange rises to 41. The exchange said it has added 325 new ETF listings so far this year.

data.title: Why the recent market rebound may only be temporary
data.description:
US stocks have experienced a meaningful rebound in recent sessions as buyers returned to names that had given them the most trouble.

Nasdaq 100 is up significantly at writing versus its low early on Nov. 25. The bounce demonstrated that investors remain willing to aggressively load up on AI stocks after a steep decline.

But the sustainability of the latest surge depends on whether artificial intelligence companies can turn their spending on chips and data centers into enough profit to justify premium multiples.

And recent research gives investors reason to question how much they are paying.

A sharp bounce can leave most of the damage intact

Nvidia gained 4.7% in Friday’s premarket, but its last closing price was still more than 37% below its October record. A stock down that far needs to rise roughly 60% just to get back to its old high.

That gap helps explain how a rally can look dramatic on a trading screen while leaving the broader selloff largely intact.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were still on course for their worst November since 2008, even as both headed for their best week since August.

“The questions that caused the market panic are still unanswered,” XTB research director Kathleen Brooks told Reuters.

Friday’s shortened session could also mean lighter trading, leaving the rebound to face a fuller test next week.

The bubble study’s most telling finding goes beyond 97%

Researchers at “London Business School” and the “University of Cambridge” used nearly 796,000 articles from The Economist to build a gauge of speculative excess.

One model put the odds that AI shares were in a bubble at 97%, while two others put them near 40%.

The wide gap shows how much the estimate depends on the model. The finding that matters more for the rebound is what happened after the gauge rose historically.

Nasdaq returns tended to be weaker over the following year, even after accounting for valuations.

That leaves room for sharp rallies along the way. But it also suggests that shares can look cheap compared with their October highs while still offering disappointing returns from here.

The next test is whether AI spending pays for itself

A data center can be valuable to customers while delivering a thin return to the company that paid to build it.

The amounts that cloud providers spend on chips, electricity and financing will matter alongside how much customers actually pay for AI services.

If usage grows but providers have to cut prices to fill capacity, revenue can climb while profit margins shrink.

Borrowing adds pressure, especially with traders already pricing in a December Federal Reserve rate hike. That makes the next round of earnings a more consequential test than Friday’s rebound.

Investors will get to see whether the companies committing billions to AI are generating enough cash from it to support that spending.

data.title: Micron stock is highly undervalued as the Wyckoff Theory takes shape
data.description:
Micron stock has slipped into a bear market this month and now appears to be in the Wyckoff theory's markdown phase, even as its key valuation metric has fallen to bargain levels. MU was trading at $601, about 52% below its year-high. So, is this a good time to buy the dip, or should investors sell the rip?

Micron stock has become highly undervalued

In theory, companies that are seeing substantial revenue and profit growth should receive premium valuations. Some of the most popular companies that have always had a premium valuation are Walmart, Costco, and Shopify. 

Micron, however, is doing the opposite. Its revenue growth is soaring, and analysts expect the momentum will continue. The most recent results showed that its fourth-quarter revenue jumped by 379% to $54.2 billion, with its annual figure hitting $133.2 billion. Most of this growth was in its DRAM division, which made $39.8 billion. 

Micron is also a highly profitable company, with the gross margin of all its businesses being over 80%. Its total gross profit margin rose to 87%, much higher than most companies, including Nvidia. 

Most importantly, analysts believe that the company has more room for growth. For example, the first-quarter revenue is expected to hit $61 billion, while the second-quarter figure will soar to $66 billion. Its annual revenue is expected to jump by 106% to $275 billion. 

For a company experiencing this growth, its valuation metrics are significantly low. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio stands at just 3.43, much lower than the sector median of 18. 

Similarly, the company has one of the highest rule-of-40 metrics. This multiple is calculated by adding its revenue growth and its profit margins. Micron has a forward revenue growth of 106% and a profit margin of 64%, giving it a multiple of 170%. 

These metrics explain why the company is planning to accelerate its share repurchases in the near term. Its plan is to start a $35 billion program in December when the buyback restrictions end. Share buybacks help to boost a company’s earnings per share by reducing its outstanding shares.

Micron is facing risks

Therefore, the falling Micron stock price and cheaper valuation is happening because of the rising risks in the industry. One of the main risks is that the AI bubble may burst soon. The AI Stock Bubble Index has remained above 60.

There are also concerns that some AI data center companies will find it hard to survive as financing in the industry dries out. Elon Musk has warned that over 200 neocloud companies will collapse.

These fears have risen after the recent Anthropic IPO, in which the company raised over $100 billion. Its stock has plunged afterwards. OpenAI has also struggled in its fundraising. It recently raised $11 billion, much lower the $30 billion it was aiming for. 

There is also a risk that the memory supercycle will end in the coming months or years. Historically, this business is usually made up of major boom-and-bust cycles.

READ MORE: Micron, SanDisk continue their bloodbath; how long will the pain continue?

Micron share price is in the markdown phase

MU stock chart | Source: TradingView

The weekly chart shows that MU stock has formed the classic Wyckoff Method. It remained in a consolidation phase for years, a sign that it was in the accumulation phase. 

The stock then entered the markup phase mid-last year and then started its upward trend, eventually reaching a record high of $1,255. Now, there are signs that it has dropped into the markdown phase, which is characterized by panic selling.

Therefore, the stock will likely continue falling in the near term. The next key level to watch will be at the 50-week moving average of $523.

data.title: CMC Markets profit more than doubles to £106M on record first half
data.description:
CMC Markets has reported a record first half, with pre-tax profit more than doubling as its business-to-business (B2B) and institutional arms offset subdued market volatility.

The London-listed broker said profit before tax rose 115% to £106.0 million in the six months to September 30, 2026, from £49.3 million a year earlier, according to its interim results published on November 26, 2026.

Net operating income climbed 54% to £286.6 million, from £186.2 million. CMC said that beat its previous first-half record of £230.9 million, set in HY2021.

Trading revenue leads the gains

Net trading revenue rose 67% to £230.9 million and now makes up about 81% of group income, up from 74%, the company said. The institutional channel showed the fastest growth.

CMC said the record came even though the VIX volatility index stayed below its historical average for most of the period, unlike the more volatile first half of the previous year.

Net investing revenue increased 8% to £28.3 million, while net interest income rose 28% to £25.6 million, helped by active management of group and client cash.

Its Australian stockbroking business posted another record half, with net operating income up 5% to A$69.2 million.

Costs rise more slowly than income

Operating expenses rose 31% to £177.6 million, reflecting higher variable pay, expansion and technology spending, CMC said. Excluding variable remuneration, costs were £152.5 million, up from £128.4 million.

That lifted the pre-tax margin to 37.0% from 26.5%. EBITDA more than doubled to £116.5 million, and basic earnings per share rose to 29.0p from 13.3p.

The board declared a record interim dividend of 10.1p a share, up 84% from 5.5p.

CMC also completed its first £250 million Euro Medium Term Note (EMTN) issue in August, which it said was significantly oversubscribed.

Big partnerships still to come

The broker reiterated its upgraded FY2027 guidance of net operating income of at least £550 million and EBITDA of £250 million. Its financial year ends in March.

CMC said its Westpac stockbroking deal is now expected to launch in the first half of FY2028. Once live, it is expected to be the group’s largest partnership of its kind.

Staff accounts for the ASB partnership in New Zealand are live for end-to-end testing, with launch expected imminently. CMC has also expanded a deal with an unnamed neobank to provide liquidity for CFDs and other derivatives in the UK.

Dubai, warrants and crypto

CMC said its Dubai business doubled revenue between FY2025 and FY2026 and is now its fourth global hub, alongside the UK, Australia and Singapore. It has applied for expanded regulatory permissions there.

Its European warrants business has issued about 8,000 products. CMC plans an Australian warrants pilot trade before the end of 2026, having signed agreements with ASX, BNP Paribas and others.

After the period end, CMC was approved by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) as a cryptoasset business under the UK’s Money Laundering Regulations, the results statement said.

The broker has also added fractional investing, 24/5 trading in US equities and global indices, and wider options coverage to its trading platform.

“Achieving this performance against exceptionally subdued market volatility is particularly significant,” chief executive Lord Cruddas said.

“It demonstrates how far we have moved beyond a business whose performance is principally driven by the retail trading cycle,” he added. Cruddas said his recent personal share purchases of about £5 million “should underline that confidence to the market”.

CMC’s next scheduled update is its FY2027 results in June 2027.

data.title: AMD, Intel, Broadcom rally in premarket trading Friday as AI stocks rebound
data.description:
Chip stocks were rallying in premarket trading on Friday as investors bought the dip following the Thanksgiving holiday.

Intel and AMD gained roughly 4% and Broadcom jumped 3% in early premarket trading at 6:45 AM ET.

All three stocks, alongside major names in the artificial intelligence trade, have been under pressure in recent weeks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq briefly entering bear-market territory in the previous session.

Intel had shed 0.6% on Wednesday to close at $54.47, AMD had lost 1.75% to $406 while Broadcom stayed almost flat at $300.86.

The broader market was also looking set to jump, with futures linked to all three major indexes rising ahead of the shortened trading session to close the week.

However, with fundamental questions around the sustainability of the AI trade still looming, analysts are unsure whether the rebound will be durable.

"The recovery in stocks seems technical. The questions that caused the market panic are still unanswered," Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, told Reuters. "If these gains can be sustained on Friday, it would suggest that enthusiasm for the AI trade is back."

There have nevertheless been some positive developments for individual chipmakers that could help support sentiment.

Intel gets two important customer wins

Intel has secured two important customer developments that could support its manufacturing ambitions.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan announced Thursday that the company had signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P chip manufacturing process.

Intel has not disclosed the customer's identity, but the agreement marks progress in its effort to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

Separately, Microsoft became the first publicly named customer for Intel Foundry's EMIB advanced packaging technology, which will be used for Microsoft's Azure first-party silicon.

AMD jumps from Hunterbrook-triggered selloff

AMD has also made progress in its efforts to secure a larger share of the AI infrastructure market even as it struggles with allegations of links with blacklisted Chinese firms.

On November 16, AI infrastructure provider TensorWave announced a six-year agreement with OpenAI to supply 457 megawatts of dedicated computing capacity across multiple US data-center locations.

AMD has also completed its acquisitions of AI research startup World Labs, led by Fei-Fei Li, and specialised inference-chip developer Taalas.

China’s extension of the pause in controls on critical minerals till January is another good news for chipmakers, even though it is only a short-term relief.

Minerals like gallium and germanium are critical inputs in semiconductor manufacturing.

Analysts also remain bullish on the stock with TipRanks data showing 27 out of 30 analysts keeping a 'buy' rating and three suggesting 'hold'.

Broadcom has a major Anthropic deal

Broadcom has also faced significant pressure recently and investors chipped in on Friday to buy the stock, pushing it up before the opening bell.

It recently secured a significant development in its AI business through a financing arrangement involving some of Wall Street's biggest financial institutions.

Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley announced a $63 billion financing structure in October to fund the purchase of Broadcom's custom AI accelerators and networking equipment for Anthropic.

Several Wall Street firms, including StoneX, UBS, and Rosenblatt have reiterated their Buy ratings on Broadcom, but some like Rothschild Redburn have also downgraded the stock with concerns over AI financing and the sustainability of earnings.

Broadcom is scheduled to report its fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 financial results on December 9, giving investors another opportunity to assess whether its AI business can sustain growth despite recent concerns about chip demand.
